title: How to Run a Family Calendar During the Holidays (So Nobody Misses the Concert)
description: Concerts, parties, school breaks and travel? Set up a family calendar for the holiday season that busy brains actually check. 7 easy steps.
intro:
December is the busiest month of the year for family calendars. School concerts, class parties, the gift exchange where everyone needs to bring something under a set amount, work events, travel, school breaks. And half of it arrives on a crumpled flyer in a backpack.

For our brains, a date that isn't written somewhere we can see doesn't really exist. Then it pops up the morning of, and we're scrambling for a festive sweater.

This is a simple way to set up one family calendar for the holiday season: one place for every date, a weekly check-in, and reminders that actually reach you. Pick the steps that fit your family.

sections.heading: 1. Pick one calendar to rule them all
sections.body:
The biggest problem is usually too many calendars: one on your phone, one on the fridge, one in your partner's head. Pick one main calendar. Every date goes there first.

A big wall calendar works great for families with young kids, because everyone can see it. A shared phone calendar works better if everyone has a phone. Many families use both: the phone for reminders, the wall for the big picture.

sections.heading: 2. Hang it where you already look
sections.body: A calendar in the hallway gets forgotten. Put the wall calendar where your eyes go every day: the fridge, beside the coffee maker or next to the door. If you see it while you're waiting for the kettle, you'll actually read it.

sections.heading: 3. Give each person a color
sections.body:
Color makes a busy calendar easy to scan. One marker color per person, plus one for "whole family." At a glance, you see that Thursday is a purple day and the kid with the purple marker has a concert.

On a phone calendar, make a separate calendar for each person and give each a color. Same idea.

sections.heading: 4. Add a 'paper to calendar' habit
sections.body:
Flyers and permission slips are where dates go missing. When a paper comes home with a date, write it on the calendar right away, then recycle the paper (or clip it to the calendar if you need it that day).

A small cup of markers and a clip right by the calendar makes this a 30-second job.

sections.heading: 5. Write the 'what to bring' too
sections.body:
Holiday events come with extras: a dish to share, a wrapped gift, a white shirt for the concert. Write the item right on the calendar next to the event. "Class party, bring napkins."

Then add a phone reminder for the night before, so there's time to find the napkins.

sections.heading: 6. Do a Sunday 10-minute check-in
sections.body:
Once a week, look at the next seven days together. Who needs to be where? What needs to be bought, washed or wrapped? Who's driving?

Keep it short and pair it with something nice, like a hot chocolate. Ten minutes on Sunday saves a lot of Wednesday-morning panic.

sections.heading: 7. Block the empty days on purpose
sections.body:
This is the step we forget. Holidays fill up fast, and our brains need rest. Mark a few days as "home day" or "nothing day" in a color of their own. When an invite comes in for that day, the calendar already has an answer.

Saying no is easier when the calendar says it for you.

sections.heading: After the holidays
sections.body: In January, flip through December and note what worked: which events you loved, which ones were too much. Write a short note on the next year's calendar page for November. Future you will be very grateful.

outro:
A holiday calendar doesn't need to be fancy. One spot, a few colors and a weekly look-ahead keep the whole family on the same page, and leave room for rest.
